# Project 1: Drone Visual-Inertial Navigation Pipeline {#sec-project1}

A small quadrotor flies over a floor mat covered in AprilTags. A downward-looking camera photographs the mat, an onboard detector finds the tags, and an IMU reports angular rate and specific force fifty times a second. Somewhere downstream a flight controller wants to know, at every one of those fifty ticks, where the vehicle is, how it is oriented, how fast it is moving, and how much it should believe those numbers. Project 1 builds everything in between.

``` text
camera image --> tag detector (given) --> corner pixels
                                              |
                             perception model: PnP (Part B)
                                              |
                       pose measurement z + noise model R (Part B)
                                              |
IMU (50 Hz) --> mechanization (Part A) --> navigation filter (Part C)
                                              |
                       x_hat, P at IMU rate --> what a controller needs
```

The camera is the perception front end: it turns photons into a pose, and Part B asks you to build that perception model and, just as importantly, to characterize how wrong it is. Navigation lives in the middle of the stack, where a measurement model with honest noise statistics meets a motion model driven by the IMU. The controller at the bottom does not care how clever your filter is. It needs a smooth, high-rate, correctly-referenced state with a covariance it can trust, including during the stretches when the camera sees nothing. Keeping that consumer in mind is what separates a navigation engineer from someone who fits curves to data.

The project has three staged checkpoints that build one system, not three mini-projects:

- @sec-project1a: IMU dead reckoning, the inertial backbone and its error growth.
- @sec-project1b: the AprilTag PnP perception model and its measurement noise.
- @sec-project1c: three navigation filters (EKF, UKF, particle filter) that fuse A and B, compared honestly.

## Project Summary {#sec-project1-project-summary}

Project 1 is the largest project in the course and is worth **50% of the course grade**. You will build a complete visual-inertial navigation pipeline around a real quadrotor dataset, starting from raw packets and ending with fused estimates and an engineering report you can defend.

+------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+
| Checkpoint       | Focus                                                                    | Recommended pace |
+==================+==========================================================================+==================+
| Project 1a       | IMU characterization, forward mechanization, and dead reckoning          | Week 3           |
+------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+
| Project 1b       | AprilTag map geometry, PnP pose estimation, and measurement noise        | Week 5           |
+------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+
| Project 1c       | EKF, UKF, and particle-filter fusion with consistency checks             | Week 8           |
+------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+
| Complete project | Cross-method evaluation and the written report                           | Week 9           |
+------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+

The engineering goals are correctness of the math and implementation, frame and state conventions that stay consistent from the first line of code to the last plot, uncertainty models that are measured rather than guessed, and an evaluation that compares dead reckoning, visual measurements, and fused estimates against truth. A folder full of plausible-looking plots is not the goal. A pipeline whose assumptions, interfaces, noise models, and failure modes you can explain without hand waving is.

## Logistics {#sec-project1-logistics}

**Pace and deadline.** The weeks in the table above are a recommended pace that lines up with the lectures, not deadlines. Everything is due by the **end of week 16** (@sec-syllabus-course-policies). Submitting a checkpoint early for feedback is encouraged; feedback in week 4 is worth more than feedback in week 16.

**Submission.** Submit Project 1 once, on Canvas, as two files: a single-column **report PDF** (structure and expectations in @sec-intro-project-guidance) and a **code archive** (`.zip`) containing your `drone_pipeline` package with your implementations, any scripts or notebooks you used, and a short `README` that lists the exact commands that reproduce every figure and table in the report. If the grader cannot regenerate a number, it does not count as evidence.

**Environment.** From the repository root:

``` bash
uv sync                                          # install Python and the packages
uv run python scripts/fetch_data.py drone-data   # download the data (about 570 MB)
uv run pytest projects/drone_pipeline            # starter tests: support code passes, your stubs skip
uv run python -m drone_pipeline.cli 1            # quick look at studentdata1
uv run python -m drone_pipeline.run_all          # run every stage you have implemented so far
```

**AI tools and libraries.** The course policy is in @sec-intro-ai-policy-and-dependencies, including the rule for pre-built filtering libraries such as `filterpy`.

**Reusing book code.** You may adapt code from the course chapters (for example the PnP helpers in @sec-pnp or the filter skeletons in the filtering chapters) as long as you cite the section you adapted it from in a code comment and in the report. Grading rewards evidence and analysis: copied code that runs earns little; code you can justify, test, and break on purpose earns a lot.

## Project Architecture {#sec-project1-project-architecture}

``` text
load_drone_dataset(i), load_drone_parameters()
        |
        +--> Part A: propagate_state(...)          dead reckoning, IMU noise model
        |
        +--> Part B: build_apriltag_corner_map()   tag geometry
        |            estimate_pose(...)            PnP -> PoseObservation per packet
        |            estimate_measurement_covariance(...)  R (and the bias, separately)
        v
Part C: EKFNavigator / UKFNavigator / ParticleFilterNavigator
        |
        v
run_all: RMSE, NIS/NEES, runtime tables and plots -> your report
```

All three checkpoints share the same dataset, timing conventions, and state definition. If those interfaces drift between Parts A, B, and C you are no longer building one navigation pipeline; you are running three incompatible experiments.

## Shared Dataset {#sec-project1-shared-dataset}

`uv run python scripts/fetch_data.py drone-data` places `studentdata0.mat` through `studentdata7.mat` and `parameters.txt` in `data/drone-data/`. Load a dataset by index (or by path) and the parameters with:

``` python
from drone_pipeline.datasets import (
    interpolate_vicon_truth,
    load_drone_dataset,
    load_drone_parameters,
)

dataset = load_drone_dataset(1)      # data/drone-data/studentdata1.mat
params = load_drone_parameters()     # parses data/drone-data/parameters.txt
truth = interpolate_vicon_truth(dataset)
```

Each dataset holds a `vicon` array (`12 x N`, about 100 Hz), its timestamps `time`, and a list of sensor packets. The Vicon rows are:

| Rows | Quantity |
|---:|---|
| `0:3` | position `[px, py, pz]` of the body origin in the world frame (m) |
| `3:6` | roll, pitch, yaw in the dataset's Z-X-Y sequence (rad) |
| `6:9` | velocity in the world frame (m/s) |
| `9:12` | body angular rate (rad/s); it tracks the gyro |

Each packet is a `DronePacket` with these fields:

+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Field           | Shape          | Meaning                                                                             |
+=================+================+=====================================================================================+
| `t`             | scalar         | packet timestamp (s), on the same clock as the Vicon `time`                         |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `id`            | `(n,)`         | IDs of the `n` AprilTags detected in this frame (empty when none)                   |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `p1` ... `p4`   | `(2, n)`       | corner pixels `[u; v]`: bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, top-left;             |
|                 |                | **already undistorted** (see @sec-project1b)                                        |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `p0`            | `(2, n)`       | tag-centre pixels (the mean of the four corners); `None` in `studentdata0`          |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `omg`           | `(3,)`         | gyro body angular rate (rad/s); in `studentdata0` this slot holds that file's       |
|                 |                | `drpy` signal, whose meaning is unresolved                                          |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `acc`           | `(3,)`         | accelerometer specific force, body frame (m/s^2); about `+9.8` on `z` in hover      |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `rpy`           | `(3,)`         | the drone's *onboard* attitude estimate (Z-X-Y); see the truth-usage rules          |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `img`           | `240 x 376`    | grayscale camera image; you do not need it, the detections are provided             |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `is_ready`      | bool           | onboard ready flag (`studentdata1`-`7` only; always true)                           |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `rate_field`    | str            | which raw field filled `omg`: `"omg"` or `"drpy"`                                   |
+-----------------+----------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

`packet.drpy` still works as a read-only alias of `packet.omg` for older code. In `studentdata1`-`7` packets arrive at about 50 Hz (median spacing 0.020 s, longest gap 0.04-0.08 s); never assume a constant time step. Several flights begin and end with a second or more in which no tag is visible, because the drone is parked beside the mat or sitting too close to it. That is normal, and your pipeline must handle missing visual measurements cleanly rather than treating them as a software emergency.

`interpolate_vicon_truth` returns one `TruthSample` per requested time. Times outside the Vicon span come back as NaN with `valid=False` instead of a silently frozen copy of the first or last Vicon sample, so trim them before computing any error.

## studentdata0: Bad Truth, Unknown Signal {#sec-project1-studentdata0}

`studentdata0` is the odd one out, and it is excluded from the development split. Its packets arrive at 33 Hz with gaps up to 0.49 s, 75 of them fall outside the Vicon time span, its rate field is called `drpy` rather than `omg` (whether it holds Euler-angle rates, body rates in some other frame, or something else is an open question, GitHub issue #4), and its PnP poses disagree with Vicon by a nearly constant offset of about 12.6 cm in `x` and 0.09 rad in yaw. Some combination of a calibration change, a frame mix-up, and a timing problem is likely; nobody knows yet.

Treat it as an optional forensic exercise. If you take it on, put it in an appendix: say what `drpy` is consistent with and what it is not, quantify the truth offset, and argue whether the problem is in the truth, the sensors, or the timestamps. Good work here can support an Excellent rating for dataset understanding, but it is not required, and it must not leak into your tuning.

## Shared State and Measurement Convention {#sec-project1-shared-state-measurement}

Project 1 uses its own frames, defined in @sec-pnp: the world frame $w$ is the tag mat ($x$ down the mat, $y$ to the right, $z$ up out of the mat, origin at the top-left corner of tag 0), the body frame $b$ is the drone's IMU frame with $z$ up, and the camera frame $c$ is the optical frame ($x$ right, $y$ down, $z$ along the optical axis, pointing at the mat). Use this 15-state vector in all three parts:

``` python
x = [
    px, py, pz,          # position of the body origin, world frame (m)
    roll, pitch, yaw,    # Z-X-Y Euler angles (rad)
    vx, vy, vz,          # velocity, world frame (m/s)
    bgx, bgy, bgz,       # gyro bias (rad/s)
    bax, bay, baz,       # accelerometer bias (m/s^2)
]
```

The dataset's attitude follows a Z-X-Y Euler sequence, the one documented exception to the book's Z-Y-X convention (@sec-frames-conventions, @sec-pnp-euler-angles-project):

``` python
C_world_body = Rz(yaw) @ Rx(roll) @ Ry(pitch)   # drone_pipeline.utils.rpy_to_rotation_matrix
```

`drone_pipeline.utils.rotation_matrix_to_rpy` inverts it. If you use Z-Y-X by habit, everything will look fine in hover and quietly fall apart once the drone banks, so check this early. All angles are radians. Whenever you subtract two attitudes, wrap the residual into $[-\pi, \pi)$ (`drone_pipeline.utils.wrap_angles`); skip that and the filter will eventually produce very confident nonsense near the wrap point.

The visual measurement used in Parts B and C is the body pose

``` python
z = [px, py, pz, roll, pitch, yaw]   # PoseObservation.z
```

so the nominal measurement model in Part C is the linear selection `h(x) = x[:6]`.

## Starter Package Layout {#sec-project1-starter-package-layout}

Work in the starter package `projects/drone_pipeline/`, not in one heroic notebook:

``` text
src/drone_pipeline/
  datasets.py       loaders, parameters.txt parser, Vicon interpolation (provided)
  types.py          DronePacket, TruthSample, DroneParameters, PoseObservation (provided)
  utils.py          Z-X-Y rotations, angle wrapping, transforms (provided)
  config.py         documented defaults, tag geometry, dataset split (provided)
  evaluation.py     RMSE, NEES, chi-square bounds so everyone measures the same way (provided)
  mechanization.py  Part A: PropagationParams (provided), propagate_state (yours)
  observation.py    Part B: build_apriltag_corner_map, estimate_pose,
                    estimate_measurement_covariance (yours)
  filters.py        Part C: EKFNavigator, UKFNavigator, ParticleFilterNavigator
                    (constructors and accessors provided; predict/update yours)
  run_all.py        runs every stage on a split and writes tables and plots
tests/
  test_drone_pipeline.py   support-code tests plus tests of your deliverables
  test_handout_api.py      checks that this handout and the code agree
```

The public interfaces are:

``` python
from drone_pipeline.datasets import interpolate_vicon_truth, load_drone_dataset, load_drone_parameters
from drone_pipeline.mechanization import PropagationParams, propagate_state
from drone_pipeline.observation import (
    build_apriltag_corner_map,
    estimate_measurement_covariance,
    estimate_pose,
)
from drone_pipeline.filters import EKFNavigator, ParticleFilterNavigator, UKFNavigator
```

Keep those signatures stable; add helpers and modules freely. The tests of your deliverables skip with a "not implemented yet" message until you write the corresponding function, then start checking it, so `uv run pytest projects/drone_pipeline` is a quick sanity check as you go. Passing tests are necessary, not sufficient: they check interfaces and simple cases, not whether your navigation solution is good. `uv run python -m drone_pipeline.run_all` runs whatever you have implemented on the development split and reports the rest as not implemented; its `TUNING` block is where your noise values go.

## Truth Usage Rules {#sec-project1-truth-usage-rules}

The Vicon data is the truth reference. You may use it to evaluate error, to characterize sensors (IMU noise and bias in Part A, the PnP noise and bias in Part B), to study drift and consistency, and to compare filters. You may not use it as a recurring measurement inside the navigation solution. If your filter is secretly using Vicon as an update, that is not visual-inertial navigation; it is expensive cheating. The one sanctioned exception is the Vicon initialization that Part A allows; Part C filters must initialize from PnP alone.

The packets' onboard `rpy` estimate is in a grey zone, so here is the rule: you may use it for sanity checks and to compare initialization strategies, but **never as a filter measurement**. Its roll and pitch agree with Vicon to about a degree, but its yaw is offset by an arbitrary amount (2 to 68 degrees, depending on the flight), and fusing it would also mean fusing somebody else's undocumented filter.

## Development Split {#sec-project1-development-split}

Unless you justify another split, use:

- development and tuning: `studentdata1.mat` through `studentdata4.mat`;
- validation and reporting: `studentdata5.mat` through `studentdata7.mat`;
- `studentdata0.mat`: excluded (@sec-project1-studentdata0).

The two halves are deliberately different. The development flights are aggressive (speeds up to 2 m/s, roll and pitch up to about 22 degrees, tags visible throughout), while the validation flights are gentle, start beside the mat and (in two of the three) return there at the end, so they begin, and sometimes finish, without any tag in view. Sensor noise is a property of the sensor, not of the flight, so you may characterize the IMU on any dataset; tuning choices such as process-noise inflation, gates, and particle counts must be made on the development split. You are building a pipeline that generalizes, not one hand-tuned until it wins a beauty contest on one file.
